newsitem.title: GERMANY: Depressed German builders seen as long-term bet.
newsitem.headline: Depressed German builders seen as long-term bet.

text.p: German building firms are not likely to see significant earnings growth from their depressed home market until 1998 at the very earliest, industry analysts said on Thursday.
But they added investors could seek to benefit now from the weakness of stocks which are still languishing around lows hit after post-unification euphoria in the sector proved unfounded.
"An investor with a long-term view could start building up a position in one of these companies now," said Markus Strigl, an analyst at Duesseldorf-based Trinkhaus Capital Management.
But he warned: "Any purchases should definitely not be seen as a short-term buy...orders being acquired now are unlikely to show up in earnings until 1998 and 1999."

Once highly-rated shares in top construction groups including Holzmann AG, Hochtief AG and Bilfinger + Berger AG have slumped since 1991, when it became clear that east Germany would not provide the fast profit growth intially hoped for.
BHF Bank analyst Uwe Weinreich calculated Hochtief have since then shed some 58 percent of its value, while Bilfinger and Holzmann had lost 45 percent and 79 percent respectively.
Recent first-half earnings reports among the builders were marked by pessimism on domestic activities for the year as a whole and offered few prospects of an upturn the year after.

Such an outlook concurs with a forecast last month by the respected Ifo institute that German construction spending would fall by around two to three percent in 1997, while the ZDB German industry body forecasts a three to four percent dip.

But industry analysts are increasingly confident of a rise in activity across core areas of the sector from late-1997 onwards, led by renewed housing, industrial and commercial spending on construction.

"Oversupply in the housing market will be taken up next year, and industrial construction spending that has been postponed until the economy picks up will also prompt an increase in construction activity 1997 onwards," said Strigl.

Because of the delay involved in economic growth pushing construction spending higher, together with sector accounting practices which mean revenues are often booked a year later, domestic earnings are widely expected not to lag the wider economic upturn.
"This makes the building sector the cyclical laggard par excellence", BHF's Weinrich agreed.

But analysts warn that the outlook is not yet strong enough to warrant investment right across the sector and still argue that those firms which have managed most successfully to spread some of their earnings abroad offer the safest bet.

"Hochtief is particularly strong abroad because of its (44.9 percent) holding in Leighton Holdings," Bayerische Vereinsbank analyst Christine Nestroy said, referring to the Australian group that reported a record net profit for 1995/96 last month.
"We also see growth potential for Bilfinger abroad, but perhaps not to the same extent," she added.
Nestroy said she believed Bilfinger, which has operations in the U.S., east Europe, Australia and Asia, had already absorbed more of its capacity abroad than Hochtief had.
Strigl also gave Hochtief, which said in August first-half foreign orders surged 191 percent, as his preferred recommendation on the basis of its foreign exposure.
"But the timing of any (share) purchases is critical...it is still really hard to say when stock prices will start to take account of the 1998 earnings expectations," he added.
